title: A theory of humor elicitation.
finding: Theory (comprehension-elaboration): per authors, humor depends on the interpretation needed to see the humorous feature, the difficulty of identifying it, and the cognitive elaboration of its implications, all moderated by the perceiver's processing objectives at the time; applied to jokes, witticisms and unintended social humor.
why_for_us: Leave a beat after the punchline for viewers to elaborate implications (the apprentice's literal reading echoing in the notary's face); a viewer busy decoding legal jargon has no capacity left to elaborate.

title: Inside Jokes: Using Humor to Reverse-Engineer the Mind
finding: Book (theory): per the publisher abstract, humor evolved from a computational problem of open-ended thinking; the brain is 'bribed' with pleasure for finding and fixing its own time-pressured mis-leaps and near-misses, which we experience as funny. No experiments in the record.
why_for_us: The apprentice's literal interpretations let viewers catch a wrong inference in real time; the reward is in spotting the mistaken assumption, so make the false assumption visible first.

title: HUMOR AND INCLINATION TO LAUGH: EMOTIONAL REACTIONS TO STIMULI OF DIFFERENT DIVERGENCE FROM A RANGE OF EXPECTANCY
finding: Experiment (weight-judging paradigm, two designs): per authors, the inclination to laugh grew with the divergence of a lifted weight from the participants' range of expectancy, which was either measured or built up through prior experience with weights; both designs supported the incongruity hypothesis.
why_for_us: Even a non-verbal object can be funny if the scene first builds a clear expectancy; establish the 'normal' office routine (stamp, signature, file) before breaking it.

title: A two-stage model for the appreciation of jokes and cartoons
finding: Classic theoretical chapter proposing the two-stage (incongruity detection, then resolution) model of joke appreciation; OpenAlex record has no abstract or venue.
why_for_us: Reference point for the setup-punchline-'aha' structure; each episode's gag should give the viewer a rule that makes the twist make sense.

title: Children's Appreciation of Humor: A Test of the Cognitive Congruency Principle
finding: Experiments with children: per author, humor appreciation of jokes violating conservation/class-inclusion concepts was greatest soon after the concepts were acquired and lower both in children lacking them and in those who mastered them years earlier, supporting an optimal moderate cognitive challenge (inverted U).
why_for_us: Jokes about a freshly learned rule (e.g. a new procedure or new AI tool in the office) may land best with staff who just learned it; old, fully automatic routines may be less funny. Note: contradicted for adult joke latency by Cunningham & Derks 2005.

title: THE PERCEPTION OF HUMOR
finding: Review chapter (Ruch): presents cognitive models defining minimal conditions for humor, discusses the relevance and limitations of the two-stage incongruity-resolution model, introduces the weight-judging paradigm and questions the ascribed role of surprise.
why_for_us: Surprise alone is not a guarantee of a laugh; pair the twist with a playful, safe frame.

title: Humor and the Incongruity Hypothesis
finding: Experiment N=90 students (method of constant stimuli with weights): per authors, humor responses increased with the size of the incongruity between expected and actual comparison weight, and also with the number of judgments made before the incongruous weight, i.e. a longer build-up of expectation produced more humor.
why_for_us: Repeating a routine beat 2-3 times before the twist (e.g. the notary stamps three documents identically) should strengthen the expectation the punchline breaks.

title: Humor appreciation and latency of comprehension
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Two experiments: per authors, the relation between the latency of recognising a message as a joke and its funniness was primarily negative and linear; there was no evidence of the predicted inverted U, and funnier material was recognised faster (supporting an 'expert skill' account).
why_for_us: Contradicts the 'make them work for it' belief: for a scrolling audience, the faster a notary viewer gets the gag, the funnier it is likely to be; avoid multi-step inferences.

title: Humor by Violating an Existing Expectancy
finding: Experiment (students lifted textbooks; one was six times heavier than normal): per authors, the incongruous book evoked humor when presented first, by violating the expectancy students brought from everyday life, not only an expectancy created in the lab.
why_for_us: Notaries bring strong professional expectancies (procedure, formality); violating those existing schemas needs no setup time, which suits 60-90 s episodes.

title: Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny
finding: Five experiments (moral violation scenarios): per authors, benign moral violations elicited laughter and amusement in addition to disgust; a violation became benign via an alternative norm making it acceptable, weak commitment to the violated norm, or psychological distance, and seeing the act as both wrong and not wrong mediated behavioural displays of humor.
why_for_us: Every gag needs a small breach of office norms (a skipped formality, AI 'eating' credits) plus a cue that nobody is really harmed; the dry notary's calm acts as the 'it's okay' signal.

title: A theory of humor
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Theoretical article (Veatch) proposing a general theory of humor, the precursor cited by benign violation theory; OpenAlex record has no abstract, so its content is not summarised here.
why_for_us: Historical anchor for the 'violation + normal at the same time' idea used throughout this register.

title: Differentiating what is humorous from what is not.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Six studies (entertainment, consumer products, social interaction): per authors, incongruity is defined in at least four inconsistent ways (surprise, juxtaposition, atypicality, violation) and does not by itself separate humorous from non-humorous experiences; the benign-violation hypothesis differentiated them better, reducing false predictions that joyous, amazing or tragic situations are funny.
why_for_us: A surprising twist that is only 'amazing' (a perfect AI deed in 2 seconds) is not a joke; it needs a threat to someone's identity or norms that is simultaneously okay.

title: Too Close for Comfort, or Too Far to Care? Finding Humor in Distant Tragedies and Close Mishaps
finding: Five studies: per authors, severe violations (tragedies) were more humorous when temporally, socially, hypothetically or spatially distant, whereas mild violations (mishaps) were more humorous when psychologically close; an interaction other humor theories struggle to explain.
why_for_us: Small, relatable office mishaps (a stamp in the wrong place, the credits running out mid-deed) are funniest when they feel like 'our office'; serious harms to clients (lost deeds, fraud) need distance or should be avoided.

title: What Makes Things Funny? An Integrative Review of the Antecedents of Laughter and Amusement
finding: Integrative review of 20+ theories: per authors, of five candidate antecedents, simultaneity, violation and benign appraisals help distinguish humorous from non-humorous experiences, but surprise and superiority do not; the review aims to dispel popular but inaccurate ideas.
why_for_us: Write gags as 'wrong and fine at the same time' rather than relying on surprise or on mocking someone weaker; this is the most evidence-backed checklist for the series.

title: The Rise and Fall of Humor: Psychological Distance Modulates Humorous Responses to Tragedy
finding: Empirical article; OpenAlex record has no abstract. Title and keywords (Hurricane Sandy, temporal distance, benign violation theory) indicate that humorous responses to a real tragedy rose and fell as a function of psychological (temporal) distance; numbers not available in the record.
why_for_us: Topical jokes about a recent painful event in the profession (e.g. a real failed IT rollout) should wait until it is no longer raw; check timing with the audience.

title: You Must Be Joking! Benign Violations, Power Asymmetry, and Humor in a Broader Social Context
finding: Theoretical review/critique: per authors, benign violation theory must distinguish joke-teller and listener perspectives, their mutual social distance, and power asymmetries; power differences may explain systematically mismatched judgements of whether something is benign (e.g. in harassment, abusive supervision).
why_for_us: Senior notary mocking the apprentice can read as benign to the boss and malign to staff viewers; let the apprentice also 'win' sometimes so the power gag stays benign for the employee audience.

title: The Impact of Culture and Social Distance on Humor Appreciation, Sharing, and Production
finding: Four studies: per authors, Chinese participants appreciated and intended to share jokes about distant others more than about close others, and produced funnier captions for them; Americans showed little social-distance effect; interdependence priming produced the distance effect, independence priming did not.
why_for_us: Distance effects depend on culture; for a Polish professional audience, test whether jokes target 'a notary somewhere' versus 'you, the viewer' before scaling.

title: Smiling at moral misbehaviors: the effect of violation benignness and psychological distance
finding: Experiment with facial-expression recording and self-ratings (purity vs harm violations, second- vs third-person framing): per authors, amusement was elicited only by the more benign purity violations, judged malignance strongly predicted (less) amusement, but there was no effect of psychological distance; results 'partially support' benign violation theory.
why_for_us: Benignness matters more reliably than distance: keep the consequence of the AI gag clearly harmless rather than relying on 'it happens to someone else' framing.

title: Social Consequences of Disparagement Humor: A Prejudiced Norm Theory
finding: Theory: per authors, disparagement humor implies a norm of tolerance of discrimination that, for people high in prejudice, increases tolerance of subsequently encountered discriminatory events; it creates a normative climate rather than changing everyone's attitudes.
why_for_us: Avoid gags that mock clients by age, gender or origin even as a 'harmless' aside; for a professional audience this is a reputational and ethical risk with no comic upside.

title: Disparagement humor: A theoretical and empirical review of psychoanalytic, superiority, and social identity theories
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Review: per authors, evaluates psychoanalytic, superiority and social identity explanations of why disparagement humor is amusing and concludes that social identity theory (in-group vs out-group) is the most promising account.
why_for_us: Jokes at the expense of an out-group (e.g. 'the IT people', 'the ministry') bond notary viewers as an in-group; jokes at notaries themselves must be self-aware to stay in-group.

title: Dissing Oneself versus Dissing Rivals: Effects of Status, Personality, and Sex on the Short-Term and Long-Term Attractiveness of Self-Deprecating and Other-Deprecating Humor
finding: Two-part study, N=96 students: per authors, men reported using more other-deprecating humor than women and its use declined with age; in ratings of recorded speakers, self-deprecating humor by high-status (but not low-status) presenters increased long-term attractiveness for both sexes.
why_for_us: Self-deprecation works when the speaker has status: let the senior notary make the dry jokes at his own expense, not the apprentice, whose self-deprecation reads as low status.

title: A Disposition Theory of Humour and Mirth
finding: Theory chapter (Zillmann & Cantor; reprint in a 2017 edition of a classic volume): per authors, the intensity of mirth depends on the respondent's affective disposition toward the protagonists; humor appreciation is facilitated when the disparaged party is disliked and impaired when the respondent likes or sympathises with them.
why_for_us: Viewers must like the apprentice, so gags that humiliate him will be weaker; aim the 'put-down' at the situation, the bureaucracy or the greedy little computer rather than at a sympathetic character.

title: Judged humor, arousal, and the relief theory.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Experiment with 3 anxiety levels (students expected to handle or draw blood from a rat, which turned out to be a toy): per author, humor ratings rose significantly with induced anxiety and with surprisingness, supporting relief theory with surprise as a correlated variable.
why_for_us: Build brief real tension (a client waiting, a deadline, 'the deed won't print') and release it with a harmless reveal; the bigger the build-up, the bigger the laugh, as long as the reveal is clearly safe.

title: The (null) effects of exposure to disparagement humor on stereotypes and attitudes
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Empirical article; OpenAlex record has no abstract. Title and keywords ('null effect', stereotypes, attitudes) indicate that mere exposure to disparagement humor did not measurably change audience stereotypes or attitudes in these studies.
why_for_us: Counterweight to Hobden & Olson: watching (not telling) a disparaging joke may not shift attitudes, but this does not make such jokes funnier or safer for brand image.

title: From Jest to Antipathy: Disparagement Humor as a Source of Dissonance-Motivated Attitude Change
finding: Experiment: per authors, participants who read 12 disparaging jokes about lawyers aloud under high (vs low) choice later evaluated lawyers less favourably, an effect if anything stronger under anonymity, i.e. telling disparaging jokes can shift the teller's own attitudes via dissonance.
why_for_us: Directly relevant to legal professions: a series that has notaries repeatedly mock their own clients or profession could subtly erode how staff see them; keep self-mockery affectionate.

title: Audience reaction to self‐disparaging humor
finding: Experiment N=58 students (written 'radio' speeches): per authors, high-status speakers (professors) who disparaged their own professional field raised their ratings of wit, funniness and sense of humor without damaging other credibility factors.
why_for_us: A notary joking about notarial bureaucracy can gain warmth without losing authority; small regional venue and old sample, so treat as indicative.

title: The Game of Humor: A Comprehensive Theory of Why We Laugh
finding: Book (theory; Routledge edition of Gruner's superiority theory): per the abstract, all humor can be analysed as a game with winners and losers, extending Hobbes's superiority theory to good-natured play; argued by examples, not experiments.
why_for_us: Useful scoring lens for each scene: who 'wins' the exchange between dry notary and literal apprentice? Rotating the winner keeps the running gag fresh.

title: Humor, laughter, and physical health: Methodological issues and research findings.
finding: Systematic review of all published research on humor, laughter and physical health: per author, lab effects of comedy on immunity are inconsistent and methodologically weak; analgesic effects exist but similar effects are found with negative emotions; few health benefits are firmly established.
why_for_us: Do not promise 'laughter is the best medicine' in marketing copy for the series; the claim is not supported.

title: THE EVOLUTION AND FUNCTIONS OF LAUGHTER AND HUMOR: A SYNTHETIC APPROACH
finding: Synthetic review/theory: per authors, distinguishes spontaneous Duchenne laughter (proposed to have become ritualized 4-2 million years ago as playful emotional contagion signalling safe times, elicited by non-serious social incongruity) from later-evolved volitional non-Duchenne laughter used for strategic and 'dark side' functions.
why_for_us: Comedy works best in a frame that signals safety and play; non-serious social incongruity (the apprentice taking 'feed the computer' literally) is exactly the trigger type the theory names.

title: Not All Laughs are Alike: Voiced but Not Unvoiced Laughter Readily Elicits Positive Affect
finding: Experiment, N=128 listeners rated 50 voiced and 20 unvoiced laughs twice under five rating strategies: per authors, results were highly consistent across strategies, with voiced (song-like) laughs eliciting more positive responses than unvoiced (grunt, snort-like) laughs.
why_for_us: When a character laughs in voice, use voiced, tonal laughter to spread warmth; unvoiced snorts read as neutral or sly, which may suit the dry notary but will not lift the viewer.

title: Contagious laughter: Laughter is a sufficient stimulus for laughs and smiles
finding: Experiment (Provine); OpenAlex record has no abstract. The title states the result: hearing laughter alone (without a joke) was sufficient to elicit laughs and smiles in listeners; effect sizes not available in the record.
why_for_us: A genuine on-screen laugh (e.g. the receptionist trying not to laugh) can itself trigger viewer smiles; use sparingly and make it sound spontaneous (see Bryant et al. 2018).

title: Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
finding: Six experiments (lab video watching and live stage performances): per authors, pain thresholds were significantly higher after laughter than in control conditions, attributed to laughter itself rather than to positive affect, consistent with endorphin release supporting social bonding.
why_for_us: Laughing together bonds; episodes that are watched together in the office kitchen do more for affiliation than solo viewing, which supports a 'share with your team' call to action.

title: Laughter Punctuates Speech: Linguistic, Social and Gender Contexts of Laughter
finding: Naturalistic observation, 1200 laughter episodes in public places: per author, speaker and audience laughter occurred at pauses at phrase/sentence ends in over 99% of cases; laughter often followed statements and material not humorous out of context; speakers (especially women) laughed more than audiences, and audiences laughed more to male speakers.
why_for_us: Real laughter is mostly social punctuation, not a reaction to jokes; on screen, a character's small laugh at the end of a line (not mid-sentence) reads as natural and signals 'this is friendly'.

title: Social Laughter Triggers Endogenous Opioid Release in Humans
finding: PET study, N=12 healthy males (30 min comedy with close friends vs 30 min alone) plus behavioural control in groups: per authors, social laughter increased pleasure and triggered opioid release in thalamus, caudate and anterior insula, and pain threshold rose more after laughter-inducing comedy than drama.
why_for_us: Small sample, but converges with Dunbar 2011: comedy watched with colleagues has a physiological bonding effect; group viewing is a design goal, not a side effect.

title: Laughing, Smiling, and Talking: Relation to Sleeping and Social Context in Humans
finding: Diary study, students logged laughing, smiling and talking for one week: per authors, all three were most frequent in social situations and least likely just before bed and after waking; laughs and smiles occurred mainly during social encounters and conversations, so they are poor indices of ongoing emotional state.
why_for_us: Solo viewing on a phone suppresses laughter; design episodes to be shared (sent to colleagues, watched together in the office) and judge success by smiles and shares, not by expected laughs.

title: Detecting affiliation in colaughter across 24 societies
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
finding: Cross-cultural experiment, N=966 listeners in 24 societies: per authors, people distinguished brief co-laughter of established friends from that of recently acquainted strangers with 53-67% accuracy, and judgments were predicted by voicing dynamics associated with spontaneous production.
why_for_us: Shared laughter between characters tells viewers who is close; if the notary and apprentice laugh together at the end, the audio must sound like friends, not polite strangers.

title: The Perception of Spontaneous and Volitional Laughter Across 21 Societies
finding: Cross-cultural experiment, N=884 listeners from 21 societies, 36 recorded laughs: per authors, listeners told real from fake laughter with 56-69% accuracy, and arousal-related acoustic features predicted judgments fairly uniformly across societies.
why_for_us: AI-generated or posed laughter is likely to be heard as fake; if a laugh is used in voice-over, it needs high-arousal, spontaneous-sounding acoustics or should be cut.

title: Funniness of Jokes, Canned Laughter and Recall Performance
finding: Experiment, two groups of 30 (15 men, 15 women each), 10 tape-recorded jokes with or without canned laughter: per author, canned laughter generated more overt mirth but did not significantly affect humor ratings or 'intellectual appreciation'.
why_for_us: A laugh track may increase visible smiling without making the joke judged funnier; for a professional audience the writing must carry the gag on its own.

title: Humor Modulates the Mesolimbic Reward Centers
finding: Event-related fMRI at 3 T: per authors, humor engaged subcortical regions including the nucleus accumbens of the mesolimbic dopaminergic reward system, and humor intensity correlated positively with BOLD signal in these regions.
why_for_us: Funniness is graded reward, not a yes/no switch; a stronger payoff gag at the end of each episode is worth more than several weak ones, and reward-driven rewatching favours a punchy final beat.

title: The neural basis of humour processing
finding: Review (Nature Reviews Neuroscience); OpenAlex record has no abstract. Keywords list incongruity resolution, amygdala, reward and salience processing, sex differences, personality and children as covered topics.
why_for_us: Entry point for the lab's neuroscience background; no direct writing rule from the record.

title: Neural correlates of humor detection and appreciation
finding: fMRI study; OpenAlex record has no abstract. Keywords indicate participants watched sitcom clips (Seinfeld, The Simpsons) and that humor detection was associated with inferior frontal and posterior temporal cortex and appreciation with the insula; numbers not in the record.
why_for_us: Supports treating 'getting' a joke and 'enjoying' it as separate steps: a clear setup handles detection; the character's reaction and performance carry appreciation.

title: Sex differences in brain activation elicited by humor
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
finding: Event-related fMRI, N=20 (10 women), 70 cartoons rated funny/unfunny: per authors, both sexes recruited similar networks (temporal-occipital junction, temporal pole, inferior frontal gyrus), but women showed more left prefrontal and more nucleus accumbens activation, interpreted as more executive processing and possibly lower reward expectation.
why_for_us: Shared network matters more than the difference; one gag can serve a mixed-gender staff audience. Small N, so do not segment content by sex on this basis.

title: Humor Comprehension and Appreciation: An fMRI Study
finding: fMRI with non-verbal cartoon pairs: per authors, funny vs non-funny cartoons activated right inferior frontal gyrus, left superior and middle temporal gyri and left cerebellum, areas also used in attributing intentions; left amygdala activity tracked rated amusement.
why_for_us: Resolving a visual gag relies on reading characters' intentions; in silent AI video, make what each character wants legible (the apprentice earnestly 'feeding' the computer) so viewers can resolve the incongruity without words.

title: Effects of humor on sentence memory.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
finding: Experiments: per author, humorous sentences were better remembered than non-humorous versions in free and cued recall; the effect persisted when participants were warned humor was coming, but was attenuated in incidental learning and limited to within-subject designs; humor seems to receive more attention and rehearsal.
why_for_us: The funny line is what viewers will remember, so put the key message (e.g. 'top up credits before signing') inside the punchline; the advantage is strongest when funny lines stand out against non-funny ones.

title: Finding comfort in a joke: Consolatory effects of humor through cognitive distraction.
finding: Picture-viewing experiment: per authors, after mildly and strongly negative pictures, humorous stimuli reduced negative feelings more than equally positive non-humorous stimuli; no difference after neutral pictures; more cognitively demanding stimuli regulated negative emotion better, consistent with a working-memory distraction account.
why_for_us: A gag placed right after a stressful moment (angry client, failed upload) relieves the viewer more than a merely pleasant image, because resolving it occupies working memory.

title: Right hemisphere has the last laugh: neural dynamics of joke appreciation
finding: Anatomically constrained MEG, funny vs congruent-unfunny vs nonsensical punchlines: per authors, funny punchlines evoked the smallest N400m (surface congruity with the setup), followed by medial prefrontal 'second take' processing and right prefrontal reprocessing that links punchline and setup; nonsense endings evoked the largest N400m.
why_for_us: A good punchline should feel locally natural (fits the sentence) and only then flip meaning; a line that is simply bizarre is processed as an error, not a joke.

title: The effects of normal aging on humor appreciation
venue: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
finding: Comparison of elderly vs young adults (plus frontal-lesion patients): per authors, the elderly showed a relative deficit in cognitive comprehension of humor (choosing punchlines, cartoon arrays) that correlated with working memory, flexibility and abstraction, but intact affective appreciation and emotional reactiveness.
why_for_us: Senior notaries may miss gags that require holding several facts in mind, yet enjoy them as much once understood; keep the inference chain short and give one clear visual cue.

title: Humor comprehension in older adults
venue: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
finding: Cross-sectional study, 40 younger vs 41 older adults: per authors, older adults scored lower on verbal and non-verbal humor comprehension and on cognitive tests; regressions supported cognition affecting comprehension, though which mechanism matters most remained unclear.
why_for_us: Replicates Shammi & Stuss: for an older professional audience, simplify the logic of the gag rather than its content or tone.

title: Individual differences in uses of humor and their relation to psychological well-being: Development of the Humor Styles Questionnaire
finding: Scale development article; OpenAlex record has no abstract. Keywords name the four humor styles of the Humor Styles Questionnaire (affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, self-defeating) and their links to well-being, self-esteem, optimism and Big Five traits; coefficients not in the record.
why_for_us: Gives a vocabulary for character design: the notary's dry wit can be self-enhancing (coping), the apprentice's earnestness affiliative; avoid making either character's humor aggressive toward clients.

title: Cultural Differences in Humor Perception, Usage, and Implications
finding: Review: per authors, evidence shows Easterners hold less positive attitudes toward humor than Westerners and are therefore less likely to use humor as a coping strategy; the review covers culture's effects on humor perception, use and well-being.
why_for_us: Attitudes toward humor itself (is joking at work appropriate?) vary by culture and profession; a formal profession like notaries may share some of this ambivalence, so signal that the joke is respectful.

title: Humor ability reveals intelligence, predicts mating success, and is higher in males
finding: Empirical article; OpenAlex record has no abstract. The title states that humor production ability was associated with intelligence (keywords: verbal intelligence, abstract thinking), predicted mating success and was higher in males in this sample; numbers not in the record.
why_for_us: Wit signals intelligence: the dry notary's quick one-liners make him look smart, while the apprentice's literalism must never make him look stupid, only inexperienced.

title: The fear of being laughed at: Individual and group differences in Gelotophobia
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Questionnaire study, N=863 clinical and non-clinical participants: per authors, gelotophobes could be separated from shame-based and non-shame-based neurotics and controls (about 69% correctly classified); gelotophobia is best treated as unidimensional and varies tremendously among adults.
why_for_us: Some staff viewers will read laughter at a colleague as ridicule; show the apprentice being laughed with, not at, and give him the last word sometimes.

title: Personality predicts activity in reward and emotional regions associated with humor
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
finding: Event-related fMRI: per authors, extroversion correlated positively with humor-driven activity in right orbitofrontal, ventrolateral prefrontal and bilateral temporal cortices; introversion with bilateral amygdala; emotional stability (low neuroticism) with mesocortical-mesolimbic reward circuitry (orbitofrontal cortex, caudate, nucleus accumbens).
why_for_us: Audiences differ in how rewarding the same joke is; a conservative, introverted professional audience may need a gentler, lower-arousal style of gag.

title: To Be or Not To Be Humorous? Cross Cultural Perspectives on Humor
finding: Experiments with cultural priming and cross-national samples: per authors, Hong Kong participants primed with Western culture evaluated humor more positively than when primed with Chinese culture; Westerners treat humor as a common positive disposition, Chinese participants as a special, somewhat controversial trait of humorists.
why_for_us: Whether being funny is seen as a virtue or a risk can be primed by context; framing the series as professional in-group content may make humor feel legitimate to serious viewers.

title: Breaking ground in cross-cultural research on the fear of being laughed at (gelotophobia): A multi-national study involving 73 countries
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Cross-cultural survey, N=22,610 in 93 samples from 73 countries (42 languages): per authors, the 15-item GELOPH was reliable everywhere (mean alpha .85) and unidimensional; item endorsement ranged from 1.31% to 80%, and score variation tracked national culture more than language.
why_for_us: Fear of ridicule differs by culture; a Polish sample was part of the study (University of Warsaw co-author), so the Polish norm can be looked up before pushing 'laughing at' humor.

title: Sex differences in humor production ability: A meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of sex differences in humor production ability; OpenAlex record has no abstract, so the direction, size and k are not stated here (keywords include publication bias).
why_for_us: Do not cast 'who is the funny one' by gender stereotype; check the full paper before using any figure.

title: A cross-cultural study of humor appreciation: Italy and Germany
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Cross-national study, 148 Italian vs 148 German adults with the 3 WD humor test: per authors, the taxonomy of incongruity-resolution, nonsense and sexual humor replicated in Italy; Italians appreciated sexual humor more and nonsense humor less than Germans.
why_for_us: The resolvable-incongruity vs nonsense distinction is a stable axis of taste; national audiences differ in their tolerance for pure nonsense, so do not assume absurd AI imagery will travel.
